1	# S108 Part A: the frozen template
2	
3	*The same template for the four agents of Part A (decision S52). Built by `tools/s108_build.py` from the text and the formal core after the fourth review round and from the frozen set (`tools/s108_frozen_set.py`). The frozen set is the drafters' working reading of "the parts that are hard to vary"; the owner has not been asked to approve it. Nothing here changes the text or the maths: Part A varies copies.*
4	
5	## 1. How to read it
6	
7	- Every sentence of the text and every definition and encoding of the formal core carries one mark:
8	  - **FROZEN**: a part that is hard to vary, in the working reading: it was put to the readers or checkers at least once (challenged or tested), and no round or step changed it. It stays exactly as it is in every variant. Why each item is frozen: `the frozen set.md` beside this file.
9	  - **S1**, **S2**, **S3**, **S4**: the middle, in four sections. Each agent varies its own section only.
10	- Ids: a sentence unchanged since the oldest text the record follows sentence by sentence is `L<line>.s<k>`; a sentence whose words are newer is `L<line>.n<k>`; a display formula carries the line of its `\[`. Definitions are `D§.n`, encodings `En`, as in the formal core.
11	- A frozen sentence whose definition is in the middle constrains that definition: a variant of the definition must still be a reading of the frozen words. A frozen definition whose sentence is in the middle is the maths those words now point to.
12	
13	## 2. The four sections
14	
15	| section | Parts | lines | middle sentences | middle definitions | frozen items in its stretch |
16	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
17	| S1, the opening, organizations, kinds and questions | Part 0 to Part III | L1–L164 | 145 | 9 | 57 |
18	| S2, transports, provenance, account and conflict | Part IV to Part VII | L165–L350 | 130 | 23 | 95 |
19	| S3, criticism, construction, repair and the physical module | Part VIII to Part XII | L351–L484 | 119 | 18 | 49 |
20	| S4, recursion, the class, what would rule it out, and the Arguments | Part XIII to Part XVI | L485–L632 | 125 | 8 | 37 |
21	
22	A definition belongs to the section of the Part whose lines it formalizes (the lines it quotes); one that quotes none belongs by its section of the core. The middle definitions of each section:
23	
24	- **S1**: D0.2, D1.4, D2.1, D2.4, D2.6, D3.3, D3.4, D3.6, D4.6
25	- **S2**: D5.7, D6.3, D6.4, D6.5, D6.7, D6.8, D6.9, D7.4, D8.2, D8.new1, D8.3, D8.5, D9.8, D10.3, D10.6, D11.2, D12.1, D12.2, D12.3, D12.7, D12.8, E1, E2
26	- **S3**: D9.1, D9.2, D9.4, D9.6, D9.7, D9.9, D9.10, D11.3, D11.4, D13.3, D13.7, D13.8, D14.1, D14.7, D15.1, D15.2, D15.5, D15.8
27	- **S4**: D12.9, D16.3, D16.4, D16.5, D16.XV, E9, D18.1, D18.2
28	
29	## 3. The text, sentence by sentence
30	
31	Each line: `id | mark | the sentence`, in the order of the text; headings as they stand. A sentence longer than 1,500 characters is cut at a space, the later pieces marked `(cont.)`.
32	
33	
34	# Claude Fable Semantics
35	
36	
37	## A structural class of explanatory creativity, with selected and constructed correspondence
38	
39	
40	# Part 0 — Read this first
41	
42	`L8.n1` | S1 | **Two words, as used here.** An **argument** is reasons why this and not that: something that can be strung together into a coherent structure to decide why this and not another.
43	`L8.s2` | S1 | Each of its steps is of an inference form that the person using it admits (\(\operatorname{Form}_j\), Part IX), and admitting a form, like accepting a claim, is tentative; for that person, while the form stays admitted, the step rules out the case in which its premises are met and its conclusion fails.
44	`L8.s3` | S1 | An argument rules out a claim when the claim is inconsistent with its conclusion and the claim's denial is not among its premises, in the structural sense of Part IX.
45	`L8.s4` | S1 | An argument is never a reason *for* a claim: what it does is rule out a claim's denial, or a rival, for someone who can use it, and only while it stays usable (K2).
46	`L8.s5` | S1 | A claim that no argument rules out is only not ruled out, and gets nothing from that; a claim whose denial an argument rules out gets nothing more than that ruling out.
47	`L8.n6` | S1 | To **tentatively accept** a claim is a person's choice to go on with it, made for whatever reason; whatever is accepted is accepted tentatively, open to being dropped, and the semantics never defines accepting by the arguments someone holds.
48	`L8.s7` | S1 | A premise of an argument can be a claim tentatively accepted as given, and an argument need not cite a test (Part IX).
49	`L8.n8` | S1 | Nothing in the semantics is settled: whether a candidate meets the conditions of an account depends on the candidate, its question and its target, not on anyone's view of them, and whatever anyone accepts about it is accepted tentatively (Part VI); a theory is never settled.
50	`L8.n9` | S1 | Where a claim taken as given is used to rule out a rival, that ruling out is a choice the person made, not something the claim does by itself.
51	
52	## What this document claims
53	
54	`L11.s1` | S1 | An explanation is a **question-relevant organization of dependencies**, held to a target by a **transport** that is tested only by **what changes when things are changed**.
55	`L11.s2` | S1 | The definition never asks whether a piece of the explanation "is the same kind of thing" as a piece of the world.
56	`L11.s3` | S1 | That question has no independent content: at any level of detail, a *kind* is nothing over and above how a component responds to the changes that level admits.
57	`L11.s4` | S1 | Two components no admitted change can separate are one kind at that level, whatever labels anyone attaches to them (Part II, Argument 1).
58	`L13.s1` | S1 | Correspondence between a representation and what it represents is not an import here.
59	`L13.s2` | S1 | It is a **relation with a provenance**.
60	`L13.s3` | S1 | A correspondence can be *selected*, produced by variation and survival on a history of encountered changes, with no represented target in that history; or *constructed*, produced by an episode of conjecture and criticism; or merely *declared* by whoever writes the model down.
61	`L13.s4` | S1 | The three are told apart by their histories, not their outputs, and the semantics keeps them apart (Part IV).
62	`L13.s5` | S1 | Creativity lives in construction.
63	`L13.s6` | S1 | Selection produces the raw material construction works on.
64	`L13.s7` | S1 | Declaration is used only as a modelling convenience, and a claim about creativity cannot depend on it.
65	`L15.s1` | S1 | Questions have provenance too.
66	`L15.s2` | S1 | A question, meaning its target, its scope of admitted changes and what it asks, can be found as well as answered, and the semantics represents both (Part III, Argument 5).
67	`L15.s3` | S1 | This is what separates it from any class in which questions are inputs: such a class cannot represent question-finding, and creativity includes finding questions, not only answering them.
68	`L17.s1` | S1 | The **constitutive conjecture** is this: explanatory creativity is fully characterized by (i) organizations and the changes they admit, (ii) transports between organizations tested by change-fidelity alone, (iii) the provenance of those transports and of the questions they serve, and (iv) their physical realization, the instantiation and transformation of these contents in carriers (Part I).
69	`L17.n2` | S1 | A candidate would conflict with the conjecture if an argument not using these four ruled out the claim that it is a non-explanation of its question while these four cannot represent it; so would a candidate that meets \(\operatorname{Account}(\mathcal E)\land\neg\operatorname{Dec}(t)\) on its question and contract (Part V) when such an argument rules out the claim that it is an explanation there.
70	`L17.s3` | S1 | An argument that exhibits either rules the conjecture out for whoever can use it, while it stays usable.
71	`L17.s4` | S1 | Part XV lists what such an argument would have to exhibit.
72	
73	## What this document does not claim
74	
75	`L21.s1` | S1 | It does not define reference in terms of uninterpreted matter.
76	`L21.s2` | S1 | It defines reference in terms of matter **plus a selection or construction history**.
77	`L21.s3` | S1 | Physics says what organization a lump of matter instantiates; history says how that organization came to track another.
78	`L21.s4` | S1 | Neither alone yields representation.
79	`L23.s1` | S1 | It does not say prediction is explanation.
80	`L23.s2` | S1 | Fidelity is over **component structure under change**, not over outputs.
81	`L23.s3` | S1 | Two systems with identical outputs and different internal routes are different organizations here, and the semantics says so (Argument 9).
82	`L25.s1` | S1 | It does not supply an aesthetics independent of any declared appraisal, a probability on claims, an appraisal of its own, or a function that orders explanations or thinkers.
83	`L25.s2` | S1 | Where a claim needs one of these, the semantics does not supply it and marks the place: a claim that invokes an appraisal or aesthetic value takes the appraisal relation as an input (Parts XI, XIV), and a claim that needs any of the others is left open (Part XIV).
84	`L25.s3` | S1 | It does not attribute an achievement to contributors beyond what a history contains (Part XI).
85	`L27.s1` | S1 | It does not decide whether any human, machine, institution or lineage belongs to the classes defined.
86	`L27.s2` | FROZEN | It defines the classes.
87	
88	## What is imported, what is an index, and what is defined
89	
90	`L31.s1` | S1 | The semantics has two imports: the **physical module** \(\Theta\), which says what organization a physical occurrence instantiates at a grain, and the **appraisal relation** \(\mathcal N\), taken as an input wherever a question invokes an appraisal.
91	`L31.s2` | S1 | Grain, boundary, continuity and the contract of admitted changes are **declared indices**: every claim is relative to them, and none is a predicate that a case meets or fails.
92	`L31.s3` | S1 | Everything else is defined in terms of the two imports, the structural vocabulary of (O) and (Q), the declared indices and the **declared inputs**, in the order Part XIV states.
93	`L31.s4` | S1 | No undefined predicate that says "explains" without a question and a contract, or "is a cause", is taken as an import, and no definition depends on one (Argument 6); (EX) is a defined relation of an episode, not such a predicate.
94	
95	## Grievances, anticipated
96	
97	`L35.s1` | S1 | Each answer points at the part of the document that carries it; the front matter states nothing the body does not state more exactly.
98	`L37.s1` | S1 | **1. "Without declared kinds you cannot tell a cause from a correlation."** You can, and only this way.
99	`L37.s2` | S1 | A correlation has no component that responds to an intervention on its supposed input; a cause does.
100	`L37.s3` | S1 | That is a difference in edit-response, which is what the semantics asks about (Part II, "Kinds are edit-signatures").
101	`L37.s4` | S1 | A declared label adds no discriminating power: where a separating change exists, fidelity finds it; where none exists, the label asserts a distinction the level does not contain.
102	`L39.s1` | S1 | **2. "So this is operationalism: a thing is what you can do to it."** A *kind* is what a level's admitted changes can distinguish.
103	`L39.s2` | S1 | A *content* is a whole organization, which can contain components that no change at that level separates, and then they are one kind *at that level*, which is what that level contains, not a loss.
104	`L39.s3` | S1 | At a finer level with more admitted changes they may separate.
105	`L39.s4` | S1 | Every kind-claim is indexed to its level.
106	`L39.s5` | S1 | That is scoping, not operationalism.
107	`L41.s1` | S1 | **3. "If correspondences are selected, you have made fidelity a matter of survival."** No. Selection produces a transport.
108	`L41.s2` | S1 | Whether that transport is faithful on changes it was never selected against turns on the transport and the target alone, not on whether it survived.
109	`L41.s3` | S1 | Argument 3 says that a selected transport is underdetermined by its history on an unseen change wherever its population admits a differing survivor there.
110	`L41.s4` | FROZEN | Survival is how the transport got there; fidelity is what it is.
111	`L43.s1` | S1 | **4. "Then everything is relative to a contract of admitted changes, and nothing is independent of the modeller."** A contract is a stated subset of the changes its target admits (Part II), which are changes in whatever the target is, a garden, a mathematical structure or a melody, and not only those anyone could carry out.
112	`L43.s2` | S1 | An account is scoped to its contract and says so.
113	`L43.s3` | S1 | Within any contract, whether a transport is faithful at a pair turns on the transport and the target, and no assessor appears in (E).
114	`L43.s4` | S1 | A contract that quietly excludes changes its target admits to protect an account is not caught by a rule about intentions; it is caught by the requirement that the exclusion be stated (non-vacuity, Part V), and then by any criticism that supplies the excluded change.
115	`L43.s5` | S1 | What is independent of the modeller lies in the target and in fidelity; what the modeller chose to leave out lies in the stated scope, and so in the record.
116	`L45.s1` | S1 | **5. "This is teleosemantics, structural realism or functionalism with new words."** It shares commitments with each and differs from each.
117	`L45.s2` | S1 | From teleosemantics it takes the idea that a correspondence has a history; it differs by distinguishing selected from constructed histories and locating creativity only in the latter.
118	`L45.s3` | S1 | From structural realism it takes structure-preservation; it differs by making preservation change-driven and component-level, and by refusing a global isomorphism requirement.
119	`L45.s4` | S1 | From functionalism it takes substrate-independence; it differs by imposing physical realization conditions at every attribution.
120	`L45.s5` | S1 | Whether the combination is new is a question about the literature.
121	`L47.s1` | S1 | **6. "You have replaced explanation with evolution."** Selection appears at the bottom: in the arrangement Part IV describes, as one possibility and not a requirement, it produces the object layer of persistent things that explanation operates on.
122	`L47.s2` | FROZEN | Construction is a separate provenance with a separate trace, and every creative attribution requires it.
123	`L47.s3` | S1 | Nothing about construction is reduced to selection; Part IV keeps the two apart by what their histories contain, and Part XV names what an argument would have to exhibit to rule that out.
124	`L49.s1` | S1 | **7. "Mathematics has no interventions."** An admitted change need not be a physical intervention.
125	`L49.s2` | S1 | Removing a starting assumption, dropping a constraint or changing a dimension are edits on an organization, and fidelity under them is well defined.
126	`L49.n3` | S1 | A piece of mathematics explains, relative to a question, when \(\operatorname{Account}(\mathcal E)\land\neg\operatorname{Dec}(t)\) (Part VII, D16.XV).
127	`L49.s4` | S1 | The same goes for a melody, where changing a note or a chord is an edit, and for a philosophical claim, where dropping a premise or a distinction is one.
128	`L49.s5` | S1 | Whether anyone could carry an edit out in a physical system bears on testing and building (Part XII), not on whether a candidate meets (F1), (F2) and (A) there, or (E) on a contract that contains it.
129	`L51.s1` | FROZEN | **8. "Where is aesthetics?"** In Part XI, as a declared appraisal relation.
130	`L51.s2` | S1 | Artistic effect, artistic purpose and aesthetic reasons get three distinct relations, and none is defined as another.
131	`L51.s3` | S1 | The semantics does not decide between rival aesthetic reasons.
132	`L53.s1` | S1 | **9. "'Selected' is as much a stipulation as 'is a cause'."** Selection is a physical history: a population, a variation operator, a survival condition and a sequence of events (Parts IV, XII).
133	`L53.s2` | S1 | Whether it occurred is a claim about the physical module, fallible as any claim about it is (Part XII).
134	`L53.s3` | S1 | A kind-label is not a claim about anything.
135	`L55.s1` | S1 | **10. "Freezing the question for assessment while letting questions change across episodes is having it both ways."** It is, deliberately, and the two ways are indexed so they cannot be confused.
136	`L55.s2` | S1 | An assessment is an event with a frozen contract.
137	`L55.n3` | S1 | An episode is a history in which every change \(C\to C'\) carries a provenance record (D13.8).
138	`L55.s4` | S1 | Argument 7 rules out a conflict between them, for whoever can use it.
139	`L57.s1` | FROZEN | **11. "Kinds exist. A rule is not a cause."** A rule and a cause differ in how they respond to changes: a rule's application changes when the rule is edited and not when the world is intervened on; a cause's assignment changes under intervention.
140	`L57.s2` | S1 | That is a difference in edit-signature (Part II), and the semantics represents it exactly.
141	`L57.s3` | S1 | What it denies is that the difference is available before the admitted changes are fixed, or independently of them.
142	
143	## Where to attack this
144	
145	`L61.s1` | S1 | The claims the rest depends on, in the order of how much falls if they fail, are stated exactly in Part XV together with what an argument would have to exhibit to rule out each.
146	`L61.n2` | S1 | In short: (Suff) sufficiency of \(\operatorname{Account}(\mathcal E)\land\neg\operatorname{Dec}(t)\) (D16.XV); (Nec) necessity (D16.XV); (Elim) the eliminability of kinds; (Prov) the two provenances and the underdetermination of selected transports at unseen changes where their population admits a differing survivor; (QF) the representability of question-finding.
147	`L61.s3` | S1 | Anything else is a detail.
148	
149	# Part I — Commitments
150	
151	`L67.s1` | FROZEN | **Faithfulness without assessors.** Whether a transport is faithful on a contract is independent of whether anyone tentatively accepts it.
152	`L67.s2` | S1 | Systems can be in error about their transports, their observations, their criticisms and their own capacities.
153	`L69.s1` | S1 | **Fallibility without error-as-work.** A theory may contain a faithful scoped dependence together with errors elsewhere.
154	`L69.s2` | S1 | What cannot count as explanation is an error in the very dependence alleged to do the work.
155	`L69.n3` | S1 | "Explanation" in this commitment means an explanatory candidate meeting \(\operatorname{Account}(\mathcal E)\land\neg\operatorname{Dec}(t)\) on its contract (Part V, D16.XV); a theory in error offered as an answer is an explanatory candidate, which ordinary usage may still call an explanation, and whether an account is easy to vary is a separate matter (Part VI).
156	`L71.s1` | S1 | **Conjecture, criticism, action.** An idea may be entertained with no argument that rules out its rivals.
157	`L71.s2` | S1 | A criticism has a target and is itself conjectural.
158	`L71.s3` | S1 | A thinker may act on an appraisal that no argument has decided.
159	`L73.s1` | S1 | **Recursive scrutiny with operative return.** Any aspect of a system's practice, a question, a contract, a transport, a method, an attention policy, can become a target, and the result must be able to change how the system proceeds.
160	`L75.s1` | S1 | **Substrate independence with physical conditions.** Any carrier may bear an organization.
161	`L75.s2` | S1 | Every attribution of an organization to a physical system is a claim that the system instantiates it, and whether a system can is a matter of physics; here and throughout, to adopt something is to take it tentatively, open to replacement, and an attribution that the adopted physics excludes conflicts with it, as a candidate can conflict with a claim (Part VI).
162	`L75.s3` | S1 | That an organization admits an edit is not a claim that the edit can be carried out or can come about, so an attribution does not conflict with a physics that excludes carrying out an edit the attributed organization admits (Parts II and III).
163	`L75.s4` | S1 | Which organizations a carrier can bear, and whether what carriers of one physical medium bear can pass to carriers of another, are matters of physics as well, and substrate independence reaches as far as contents can pass between media.
164	`L75.s5` | S1 | Where two media cannot exchange what they bear, the contents that only one of them can bear form, for a system built of the other, a barrier in the sense of Part XIII.
165	`L75.s6` | S1 | Physical possibility enters the semantics where a content is instantiated in a carrier or transformed, as when it is held, copied, taught, tested, built or performed (Parts IV and X to XIII), and it also enters as the content of claims that a candidate can conflict with (Part VI).
166	`L75.s7` | S1 | It does not define a question, its range of changes, an account or a conflict between candidates (Parts III, V, VI).
167	`L77.s1` | S1 | **Two provenances, not one.** Selection and construction both produce correspondences.
168	`L77.s2` | S1 | They are distinguished by their histories.
169	`L77.s3` | S1 | Neither is reduced to the other.
170	
171	# Part II — Organizations and their changes
172	
173	
174	## Organizations
175	
176	`L85.s1` | S1 | An organization is
177	`L87.s1` | FROZEN | \[ D=(V,(X_v)_{v\in V},J,B,A,L). \]
178	`L91.s1` | FROZEN | \(V\) is a set of ports, each with a nonempty value domain \(X_v\).
179	`L91.s2` | FROZEN | A valuation is an element of \(X_D=\prod_v X_v\).
180	`L91.s3` | FROZEN | \(J\) indexes components; each component \(j\) has a footprint \(V_j\subseteq V\).
181	`L91.s4` | FROZEN | \(B\) is a set of boundary conditions.
182	`L91.s5` | FROZEN | \(A\) is a set of admitted edits, closed under a partial associative composition with identity \(1\).
183	`L91.s6` | FROZEN | For each \(j\), edit \(a\), and boundary \(b\), the interpretation supplies
184	`L93.s1` | FROZEN | \[ L_j(a,b)\subseteq\prod_{v\in V_j}X_v . \]
185	`L97.s1` | S1 | The compatible valuations are
186	`L99.s1` | FROZEN | \[ \operatorname{Sol}_D(a,b)=\{z\in X_D:\forall j\in J,\ z|_{V_j}\in L_j(a,b)\}. \tag{O} \]
187	`L103.s1` | FROZEN | A deleted component imposes the full relation on its ports.
188	`L103.s2` | FROZEN | An edit that sets a port replaces the component assigning that port; it does not add an equation beside an incompatible one.
189	`L103.s3` | FROZEN | A changed rule is a changed component.
190	`L105.s1` | S1 | Values of ports may be paths, functions, fields, mathematical structures or histories.
191	`L105.s2` | FROZEN | Cyclic constraints are admitted.
192	`L105.s3` | FROZEN | Several solutions remain several.
193	
194	## Roles are defined, not supplied
195	
196	`L109.s1` | FROZEN | No role assignment is supplied.
197	`L109.s2` | FROZEN | A port \(v\) is an **input** under \(A\) when \(A\) contains an edit that sets \(v\) directly.
198	`L109.s3` | FROZEN | A port is an **output** of component \(j\) when its value is determined by \(L_j\) given the other ports of \(V_j\) across \(B\).
199	`L109.n4` | S1 | A port \(o\) is an **observation** when \(\exists a\in\operatorname{Alt}_j\setminus\operatorname{Slc}_j,\ m\in V_j\setminus\{o\}\) with \(\operatorname{asg}(m)\) defined and \(L_{\operatorname{asg}(m)}(a,\cdot)=L_{\operatorname{asg}(m)}(1,\cdot)\), where \(j=\operatorname{asg}(o)\) (D2.4, D2.6).
200	`L109.s5` | FROZEN | The direction of an organization is a consequence of which edits it admits, not a stipulation about which way an equation is read.
201	
202	## Kinds are edit-signatures
203	
204	`L113.s1` | FROZEN | Fix an organization \(D\) and a contract \(C\subseteq A\times B\) (Part III).
205	`L113.s2` | FROZEN | The **signature** of component \(j\) on \(C\) is
206	`L115.s1` | FROZEN | \[ \operatorname{sig}_C(j)=\{(a,b,L_j(a,b)):(a,b)\in C\}. \tag{K} \]
207	`L119.s1` | S1 | Two components \(j,j'\) are **of one kind on \(C\)** when there is a bijection of their footprints under which \(\operatorname{sig}_C(j)\) and \(\operatorname{sig}_C(j')\) coincide.
208	`L119.s2` | S1 | A kind is an equivalence class of components under this relation.
209	`L119.s3` | S1 | For two explanatory candidates (Part V), let \(E\) and \(E'\) be their organizations and \(t=(\pi,\tau,\sigma,\lambda)\) and \(t'=(\pi',\tau',\sigma',\lambda')\) their transports from \(D\), where \(\pi\) translates valuations, \(\tau\) translates edits, \(\sigma\) translates boundaries, and \(\lambda\) assigns each component of \(E\) a subnetwork of \(D\), its counterpart, with a port translation (Part IV).
210	`L119.n4` | S1 | A component of \(E\) and a component of \(E'\) are of one kind on \(C\) when their signatures, read on \(C\) through \(\tau,\sigma\) and \(\tau',\sigma'\), coincide under a footprint bijection; Argument 2 uses kinds in this sense.
211	`L119.n5` | S1 | Argument 1 makes the like comparison between an active component \(k\) of \(E\), read on \(C\) through \(\tau,\sigma\), and its counterpart \(\lambda(k)\), read on \(C\) directly with its hidden ports projected away, up to the port translation.
212	`L119.s6` | S1 | Kinds are therefore relative to the contract; a coarser contract identifies more components, and two components of one kind on \(C\) may separate on a finer contract.

408	`L301.s1` | FROZEN | \[ \operatorname{Boundary}_{E,p}=\{(v,w)\in\mathcal V^2:\operatorname{Account}(E_v,p)\neq\operatorname{Account}(E_w,p)\}. \tag{D} \]

571	`L397.s5` | FROZEN | For \(\psi\), \(X_j(\psi)\) is the set of arguments usable by \(j\) that rule out \(\psi\).
572	`L397.s6` | S3 | Where no argument usable by \(j\) rules out \(\phi\), that absence rules out nothing, neither \(\phi\) nor \(\neg\phi\).
573	`L397.n7` | S3 | An argument need not cite a test: one with no record leaf that finds, by examining a candidate, that it gives what a claim excludes (Part VI, conflict with a claim), rules the candidate out for whoever can use it, on a question about the world as on any other.
574	`L397.n8` | S3 | Where such an argument uses a claim taken as given, the ruling out is a choice the person using it made, not something the claim does by itself (Part 0).
575	`L397.s9` | S3 | **Premises taken as given.** A premise may be a claim taken as given: tentatively accepted, for whatever reason, even with no thought given to it, by someone who holds no explanation of it.
576	`L397.s10` | S3 | As to its premises, (K2) asks only that they be live for the person using the step; neither it nor anything else in the semantics asks that the person represent (R) a premise's explanation, or any part of it, before using the premise to find an error.
577	`L397.n11` | S3 | That a person can use a claim so, without containing its explanation, is a costly gamble for all creative agents; and if this were not possible, error correction could become impossibly costly to perform.
578	`L397.s12` | S3 | The semantics names the gamble and puts no measure on it.
579	`L397.s13` | FROZEN | A system can be designed that must hold the whole explanation of a premise before using it; that is a detail outside the process the semantics describes, and the semantics does not require it.
580	`L397.n14` | S3 | **A premise that is the denial.** An argument does not rule out a claim when the claim's denial is among its premises, alone or joined to other claims by "and", read structurally (D9.7) and not by logical equivalence alone; nor does an argument whose record leaf was made from a claim rule out that claim's denial.
581	`L397.s16` | S3 | Such an argument, as one against that claim, has its conclusion among its premises, as in "\(p\) because \(p\)", and does not rule that claim out for anyone.
582	`L397.s17` | S3 | A person may still drop the claim, for whatever reason (Part 0): that is the person's choice, not a ruling out, and it leaves the claim not ruled out and any problem it poses as it was (Part VI).
583	`L397.n17` | S3 | A premise taken as given differs from such a premise: it finds that the candidate gives what the premise excludes.
584	`L397.s19` | S3 | The block catches only a premise that is the claim's denial, read structurally; a premise from which a step leads to the denial, as one does from \(r\) and "if \(r\), this candidate fails (E)", is a premise taken as given, and using it is the gamble above, not a circular argument.
585	`L397.s20` | S3 | Where the premises \(j\) tentatively accepts are inconsistent, arguments from them can rule out, for \(j\), a claim and its denial alike; the semantics then says only that \(j\)'s premises conflict, and which of them \(j\) drops, if any, is \(j\)'s choice (Part 0).

633	`L435.s1` | S3 | **Repair.** The contribution \(\Delta\) of a repair is a subhistory together with the changes of content it makes.

635	`L437.s1` | FROZEN | \[ \operatorname{Repair}_{O,P}(\xi,\xi';\Delta)\iff\exists o\in O[\neg o(\xi)\land o(\xi')]\land\forall r\in P[r(\xi)\Rightarrow r(\xi')]\land\operatorname{ProducedBy}(\Delta,\xi,\xi';O). \tag{P} \]

644	`L445.s1` | S3 | \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{CreateEx}(s,\Delta,h,e)\iff{}&\operatorname{CreativeCriticalEpisode}(s,\Delta,h,e)\land\exists\xi,\xi'\,\bigl[\operatorname{Repair}_{O,P}(\xi,\xi';\Delta)\\ &\land\exists o\in O_{\mathrm{ex}}\,\exists c,p_c,e_c,t_c,\Gamma_c\,[e_c\preceq_h e\land\neg o(\xi)\land o(\xi')\land\operatorname{Origin}_{\beta,\ell}(s,c,p_c,h,e_c)\\ &\quad\land\operatorname{Account}\big((c,p_c,t_c,\Gamma_c)\big)\land c\in\operatorname{Result}(\Delta)\land\operatorname{Deploy}_{\beta,\ell}(s,c,\xi';U_c)\land\operatorname{ProducesVia}(\Delta,c,o;\xi,\xi')]\bigr]. \end{aligned}\tag{EX} \]

656	# Part XII — The physical module
657	
658	`L461.s1` | S3 | **Tasks.** A substrate is a physical system; an attribute a set of its states; a task a specified input-to-output attribute transformation with explicit resources and side effects.
659	`L461.s2` | S3 | Possibility is the absence of a law-imposed limit, short of exact, on the tolerance to which a task can be performed and retained; it is not one trajectory that performed the task.
660	`L461.s3` | S3 | The physical module adopts a task-based formulation of physics for this purpose.
661	`L461.s4` | S3 | It is where physical possibility enters the semantics as instantiation and transformation; it also enters as the content of claims a candidate can conflict with (Part VI).
662	`L461.s5` | S3 | The module says which organizations a carrier can instantiate, and which transformations of a content, such as holding, copying, teaching, testing, building or performing it, can be carried out.
663	`L461.s6` | S3 | It does not define a question, an account or a conflict between candidates (Parts III, V, VI).
664	`L463.s1` | S3 | **Retained realization.** For protocol \(\pi\), task \(T\), constructor attribute \(C\), and enabling conditions \(\chi\),
665	`L465.s1` | FROZEN | \[ \operatorname{RetReal}(\pi,T,C;\chi)\iff\forall z\in C\ \forall i\in\operatorname{dom}T\ \forall\eta\in\operatorname{Exec}(\pi,z,i;\chi),\ \eta\text{ completes with }o\in T[i]\text{ and }z'\in C. \tag{CT1} \]
666	`L469.s1` | FROZEN | Execution families are nonempty on admitted inputs; deadlock is not a vacuous performance of the task.

668	`L471.n2` | S3 | \(F\) is monotone; \(C\subseteq F(C)\) is the invariant form; the greatest fixed point is the union of the sets \(D\) with \(D\subseteq F(D)\). (CT2)
669	`L473.s1` | S3 | **System boundary and continuity.** A capability is attributed to a system under a declared boundary (which processes and resources are the system's) and a declared continuity \(\Omega\) (what makes it the same system through change).
670	`L473.s2` | S3 | A replaced part that preserves the declared continuity leaves the same system; a process run inside the boundary is the system's whoever wrote it; a process run outside it is not the system's however close it sits.

672	`L473.s4` | S3 | Where the system's boundary is not declared explicitly, a statement that names the system and says whether a process runs inside it or outside it declares the boundary for that process; a statement that the process is the system's own, which does not say where it runs, is the attribution, not its boundary.

675	`L475.s3` | S3 | Ownership is defined by the processes and resources the boundary includes, never by the capability being attributed: "owned because it can, and can because owned" defines neither.
